20385-some-three-hundred-years-ago:
Some Three Hundred Years Ago, published in 1922, looks back to the first years of settlement on the New England coast. Long before white settlers came, Native people camped by a fresh spring close to salty shores. The spot lay some three miles from the sea.

The same spring and shore later drew white settlers to build there. The story follows that change of hands and the hard early days of the newcomers. It gives young readers a grounded picture of how a coastal settlement began, and of the people who were there before it.
20579-the-frog-who-would-a-wooing-go:
The Frog Who Would A-Wooing Go retells the old nursery tale of a frog's courtship for young readers. It begins in proper storybook style. On the quiet, sedgy bank of a stagnant pool, under the shadow of rank reeds and bulrushes, sat two frogs in earnest talk.

The two had retired from the shoal sporting in the water. The elder frog advises the younger, who is set on going a-wooing. The tale follows the famous song: the frog's visit, the mouse, and the wedding plans that end in confusion. Picture-book versions like this one kept the rhyme in the nursery.
23121-our-little-lady-six-hundred-years-:
A west door frames the past in Our Little Lady, Six Hundred Years Ago. The narrator warns how strange that world would look to modern eyes. The Dark Ages earned their name, she says, in ways the present can barely grasp. She invites readers out through the west door to picture the scene six centuries back.

Through that doorway the book leads young readers into a medieval childhood. Emily Holt specialized in such guided descents into earlier centuries, castles, convents, and manners included. Her little lady lives the history rather than reciting it. The framing device, a modern narrator picturing the scene, keeps the strangeness honest. It is a child's tour of the Middle Ages with a story for a vehicle.
as-we-go:
Charles Dudley Warner gathered twenty-eight short studies in this companion volume to As We Were Saying, drawn like it from his newspaper writing. The contents range over the whole surface of American life in the 1890s. Our President, the first piece, opens by asking how kings got started and what election does to privilege.

The rest follow his columnist's beat in no order but curiosity. The newspaper-made man, interesting girls, the tall girl, and the whistling girl treat the types of the day. Weather and character, climate and happiness, the art of idleness, and the deadly diary treat its habits. Warner's touch is light and his sentences short; these are essays to be taken one at a sitting, like the columns they were.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angola-and-co:
Also called Santa Cruz de Reino de Angola and Sao Paolo de Loanda, Angola and Congo is a diocese of Portuguese West Africa, suffragan of Lisbon. Portuguese explorers found its territory in the latter part of the fifteenth century. After 1514 it fell under the Grand Prior of the Order of Christ at Funchal in the Madeira Islands. Clement VIII made it an episcopal see in 1596.

Its peoples, Bantus, Bundas, Bushmen, and others, are said to number 2,000,000, with 1,000,000 Catholics. Father Werner's figures give them 82 parishes, plus 8 churches and 10 chapels, served by 36 priests, quoting diocesan reports to the Propaganda in Missiones Catholicae for 1888. The bishop lives at Loanda, a great seaport of 14,000, where a railway runs inland some 200 miles to Ambaca through land covered with rich plantations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-camerlengo:
Camerlengo, from the Latin camerarius, is the title of certain papal officials, since camera, chamber, meant a prince's treasure or a monastery's temporal goods. Three ecclesiastics at Rome still bear it, one for the Holy Roman Church, one for the Sacred College, and one for the Roman Clergy. The Camerlengo of the Holy Roman Church runs the property and revenues of the Holy See, succeeding the Archdeacon of Rome and the Vicedominus.

Gregory VII, himself the last Archdeacon under Alexander II, suppressed that office. Thereafter the cardinal overseeing the Apostolic Camera was called Camerarius, or in common speech Camerlengo. His office covered not only the Holy See's own goods but the fiscal rule of the Pontifical States. It included the dues paid for bulls of appointment to dioceses and abbeys.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-hyaci:
Charles-Hyacinthe Hugo was born at St. Mihiel in 1667 and died in 1739. He joined the Norbertines at Pont-à-Mousson, pronouncing vows in 1685. After philosophy and theology at Jovillier and the University of Bourges, where he became Doctor of Theology around 1690, he taught theology at Jandeures and later at Etival in Lorraine. In 1700 he became prior of St. Joseph's at Nancy, holding that post until 1713.

In 1710 Simeon Godin, Abbot of Etival, gained him as coadjutor, and Clement XI's ratification led to his installation as Abbot of Fontaine-André, in July 1712. Ten years later, when Simeon resigned, Hugo was unanimously elected abbot in his place. Digot praised his elegant, harmonious style as surpassing Dom Calmet's heavy, diffuse manner, and his 1699 refutation of Faydit on the Trinity won Paquot's praise as solid work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chicago:
A history of the Archdiocese of Chicago, which covers northern Illinois across 10,379 square miles. The story opens with the Jesuit James Marquette. He set out in October 1674 to start a mission on the Illinois River. He built a cabin at the mouth of the Chicago River, the first white dwelling on the city's site. French missionaries and traders followed, Fort Dearborn rose in 1804, and a petition of 1833 begged for a resident pastor.

Chicago became a diocese in November 1842, with William Quarter of New York as its first bishop, and an archdiocese in September 1880. Later leaders included Patrick Feehan, promoted from Nashville, and James Quigley, installed in 1903. By 1908 the archdiocese counted about 1,200,000 Catholics, 631 priests, 314 churches, and 125 city parishes with schools teaching over 80,000 pupils, alongside hospitals, orphanages, and homes for the aged poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ciudad-rodrig:
Ciudad Rodrigo, suffragan to Santiago, covers most of the province of Salamanca and part of Caceres. Its city, named for Count Rodrigo Gonzalez, who founded it around the middle of the twelfth century, holds about seven thousand people and heads its judicial district. Ferdinand the Second, King of Leon, established the bishopric, and Alexander the Third confirmed it in 1175.

The see succeeded Caliabria, a Visigothic bishopric that ran from 621 to 693. Alfonso the Eighth gave the city of Caliabria to Ciudad Rodrigo in 1191. The first bishop known with certainty was Pedro, named in 1165. The most celebrated was Don Diego de Covarruvias y Leyva, a learned jurist who held the see in 1560.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congo:
Arthur Vermeersch's entry covers the Congo Independent State and Congo missions, with an editor's note marking its date. Written before Belgium's annexation, it treats the takeover under later sections. On 20 August 1908 the Chamber approved annexation, and the Senate followed on 9 September. Belgium took the State with all rights and duties. It guaranteed allowances to Prince Albert and Princess Clementine. It created funds of $9,100,000 for Belgian public works and $10,000,000 for the king and successors.

Exploration and founding open the history, with America's share noted. International standing came through treaty recognition of the International Association. Berlin's General Act of 1885 imposed terms: free commerce for all flags, protection of natives, missionaries, and travelers, freedom of worship and conscience, postal union terms, and mediation for disputes. Missions, Catholic and Protestant, fill the later sections, with Belgian mission reviews among the sources. The entry thus joins a new state's politics to its evangelization.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diego-munoz-c: This 1913 reference article on Diego Muñoz Camargo — the Tlaxcalan chronicler. Adolph Francis Bandelier honors his famous Historia. His pen told the conquest's tale. The scholars mine his mestizo pages. The annalist of the Tlaxcalan nation. His Historia de Tlaxcala is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fargo: A 1913 entry on Fargo — the North Dakota diocese. John Shanley tells its prairie story. Its bishops serve the northern flock. St. Mary's crowns the Red River town. A see of the wheatland plains. Its 1889 erection is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-de-: A 1913 entry on Francisco de Lugo — a Spanish Jesuit of note. John Fisher records his works. The entry preserves his modest fame. His pen served the seventeenth century. A father among the theologians. His 1652 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-fran: This 1913 reference piece on Barbarigo — the Venetian cardinal. Nicholas Weber notes his famous red hat. The entry preserves his modest fame. His house served the eighteenth century. A prelate among the patricians. His 1730 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-de-lugo: This 1913 reference article on Lugo — the cardinal-theologian. Joseph de Ghellinck honors his famous tomes. His pen taught the Roman schools. The Church prized its learned son. The seventeenth century knew his name. His 1660 death is famed. His 1660 tomes are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-nicasio-: A 1913 entry on Gallego — the Spanish poet. Jeremiah Ford honors his famous verse. His muse sang the patriotic lore. The nation bless the gifted name. The nineteenth century knew his songs. His 1853 death is famed. His 1853 verse is famed. His 1853 patriotic odes are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kwango: A 1913 entry on Kwango — the Congo mission. Julian Banckaert unfolds its rugged tale. The missionaries braved the tropical wilds. The missions' foothold was dearly won. The colony knew their zeal. Its 1892 mission is famed. Its jungle chapels are famed. Its 1892 Jesuit mission is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lamego: A 1913 entry on Lamego — the Portuguese diocese. Gregor Reinhold gives its ancient story. Its bishops guard the Douro flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the Lusitanian north. Its 12th-century see is famed. Its bishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-loango: A 1913 entry on Loango — the Congo vicariate. Patrick MacAuley unfolds its mission tale. The missionaries braved the coastal wilds. The missions' foothold was dearly won. The colony knew their zeal. Its 19th-century mission is famed. Its coastal chapels are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-loyola-univer: This 1913 reference piece on Loyola University — the Chicago school. Alexander Burrowes unfolds its founding tale. The Jesuits schooled the lakeside youth. The city bless the learned name. The nineteenth century knew its halls. Its 1870 founding is famed. Its Jesuit schools are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lugo: This 1913 reference article on Lugo — the Galician diocese. Andrew MacErlean gives its ancient story. Its bishops guard the Miño flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the Iberian north. Its 2nd-century see is famed. Its bishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-miguel-hidalg: A 1913 entry on Hidalgo — the Mexican liberator. Camillus Crivelli unfolds his fateful cry. He raised the Dolores bell. Mexico hailed the fearless name. The nineteenth century told his tale. His 1811 death is famed. His 1810 Grito is famed. His 1810 Dolores cry is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-santo-domingo: Santo Domingo became the archdiocese of the New World's first see. This entry covers its archbishops, its cathedral, and its history. The primacy of the Indies: its ancient cathedral crowns the city in Hispaniola's capital in the Caribbean's isles of the Indies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simone-da-ors: Simone da Orsenigo was the architect of Milan's Duomo. This entry notes his works, his Lombardy, and his fame. The master of the marble forest: his marble spires crowned Milan in the 1390s' Duomo in the piazza of the Visconti.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tantum-ergo: The Tantum Ergo is the eucharistic hymn. This entry traces its Aquinas, its Benediction, and its music. The last verses of the Pange Lingua: their sweet music crowned Benediction in the 1200s' churches in the long naves of the abbeys.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-teofilo-folen: Teofilo Folengo was the poet of Baldus. This entry traces his macaronics, his monastery, and his fame. The Benedictine of the mock epic: his mock Baldus crowned Mantua in the 1510s' presses in the city of the very old Gonzagas.
doe-osti-3022923-icsbep-evaluation-lesso: ICSBEP got lesson-learned, and this DOE evaluation covers good practice. The pages detail the findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The practice was good. The data were nuclear. The learned were lessons. The good was practice. The evaluation was ICSBEP.
doe-osti-3484657-genesis-mission-data-pi: Big science missions generate oceans of data — and no single lab should own it all. The Genesis Mission Data Pillar report lays out a federated governance framework: rules for sharing and stewarding data across institutions. The framework keeps mission data open, fair, and usable for everyone.
el-verdugo:
Honore de Balzac's El Verdugo, The Executioner, translated by Katharine Prescott Wormeley, opens at midnight in the Spanish town of Menda during the Peninsular War. A young French officer, Victor Marchand, leans on the chateau terrace under a sky of azure, thinking deeper than military carelessness allows. The Spanish sky and the occupied town set the trap.

The townspeople rise, prisoners are taken, and Marchand returns to his general asking mercy in a voice full of feeling, to be met with bitter irony. Balzac builds the tale toward its famous horror: a son forced to serve as executioner of his own family to save one life. Written early, it is among his most concentrated tragedies.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-OregonMagazineT: nsia-OregonMagazineTomeBatesEditor Oregon Magazine Tome Bates Editor: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PolishGovernmen: A fragment survives from the May 1944 Sunday edition of PM, a New York daily newspaper. The fragment concerns the Polish government-in-exile, the wartime government working from London. It also concerns a Polish vote. The scan is fragmentary, and the article's full subject cannot be rebuilt from what remains. The scrap dates from the war's last full year, when Poland's future was being decided by armies and by governments speaking in its name.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p: In October 1993, Boris Yeltsin ordered tanks to fire on the Russian parliament building in Moscow, and the United States praised his handling of the crisis. Five years before the Archive's fuller thirtieth-anniversary account, a twenty-fifth anniversary briefing book page marked the same event under the headline of Yeltsin's shelling and Washington's superb handling quote. The evidence preserved here is the page capture alone. Its subject is the constitutional crisis that settled Russia's early democratic experiment by force, and the American approval that accompanied it.

In October 1993, Boris Yeltsin ordered tanks to shell the Russian White House, the parliament building in Moscow, crushing the lawmakers who had defied him. Thirty years later, a National Security Archive posting looked back at that crisis and at the American praise for Yeltsin's superb handling of it, quoted in the documents of the time.

The posting calls the shelling a landmark turning point in Russia's failure to build a working democracy. Force settled a fight between president and parliament, and the strongest outside power applauded rather than objected. For readers, the short account links a single violent week in 1993 to the weak democratic habits that followed, using the record Washington left behind.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_Government_C:
President Donald Trump spent many weekends at his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida, receiving guests while members and lobbyists paid for access around him. An October 2017 National Security Archive news post reports the government's latest filing in the fight over visitor records: it claimed no records system for Mar-a-Lago visitors existed at all.

That claim contradicted earlier assertions that a substantial number of records did exist, and the Archive draws out the consequence plainly. Lobbyists and foreign agents, it notes, can pay Trump clubs for unvetted access to the president. For readers, the posting captures a transparency fight at its most basic level: before anyone argues over releasing records, the government argued there was nothing organized enough to release.
half-a-life-time-ago:
Elizabeth Gaskell placed her novella Half a Life-Time Ago in a Westmorland dale between Skelwith and Coniston, at a gray stone farm under a funereal yew. Susan Dixon, a stateswoman in local speech, owns her farm and sheep-walk and keeps a house so clean that tourists praise it, yet she admits no lodger and barely a visitor. Gaskell asks what froze this capable woman into solitude.

The answer reaches back half a lifetime: a young Susan who gave up her lover to raise her orphaned young brother, and paid for the sacrifice with her whole future. When the past returns to her door in old age, duty and forgiveness face their last test. Gaskell tells it in five chapters of Lakeland weather and iron kindness.
kirsteen-the-story-of-a-scotch-family-se:
Margaret Oliphant's novel Kirsteen appeared in 1890. Its subtitle calls it the story of a Scotch family seventy years earlier. This edition was printed in two volumes in the Tauchnitz Collection of British Authors.

The long chapter list runs through two full volumes of family life. Oliphant was known for the Chronicles of Carlingford books listed here. Her fiction often examined the limits placed on women's lives. Kirsteen gives readers a wide family story set in an older Scotland, told by a skilled and popular novelist. Family duty and family pride shape the lives traced across both volumes. Oliphant handles several generations without losing the human thread.
pictures-of-jewish-home-life-fifty-years:
Hannah Trager wrote about Jewish family life in Palestine, drawing on the world she knew from her earlier books on child life there. Her sketches carry a prefatory letter by Leo Jung, four plates, and a glossary, and they were published in New York by the Bloch Publishing Company.

Chapters follow a household through the year in Jerusalem: the arrival and welcome, the baking of matzos, and the feasts of Purim, Lag B'Omer, and the Sabbath. Other pieces show how charity was given, how engagements and weddings were marked, and how the city kept the jubilee of Zorach Barnett. Together they preserve the daily customs of a home now fifty years past.
po-no-kah-an-indian-tale-of-long-ago:
Mary Mapes Dodge wrote Po-No-Kah, a frontier story for young readers published in 1903. The tale is set in a small pioneer settlement on a bend of the Ohio River, where the Hedden family farms one of the first clearings in the forest. Life there looks peaceful, with whitewashed cabins and children at play, yet the settlement lives under constant watch for attack.

Dodge opens by contrasting safe modern homes with the dangers settlers faced, when a man could return from hunting to find his cabin burned and his family taken. The Hedden household, with its wide clearing and long record of escaping harm, stands at the center of the coming trouble. The story gives young readers a vivid picture of pioneer fear and courage on the early American frontier.
podcast-dannyjones-g0y8N_jCGgo:
Ric O'Barry, the dolphin trainer who became an activist, declares his war on SeaWorld to Danny Jones. O'Barry trained the dolphins for the TV show Flipper before turning against captivity. His film The Cove exposed a dolphin hunt in Japan and won an Oscar.

O'Barry explains why he believes keeping dolphins in tanks is cruel, however clean the park. He recounts decades of protests, arrests, and campaigns against the marine park industry. Jones asks what victory would even look like after so long. Animal lovers and the indignant get the crusader's case, the Cove man's revenge for Flipper.
sketches-from-concord-and-appledore-conc:
Frank Preston Stearns wrote these sketches of Concord and Appledore, with pictures of Concord elms and the Old Manse. Contents promise Concord thirty-odd years past, then portraits in turn: Hawthorne, Louisa M. Alcott, and Emerson himself. Matthew Arnold's lecture and Wendell Phillips follow.

Appledore and the Laightons open the island half, closing with Whittier. A photograph of Alcott from 1868 stands among the pictures. Stearns knew this literary ground in person, and his pages preserve talk, faces, and places from a Concord where the great transcendental names were still living neighbors rather than statues.
the-camp-fire-girls-in-the-maine-woods-o:
Hildegard G. Frey wrote The Camp Fire Girls in the Maine Woods, or The Winnebagos Go Camping, put out in New York by A. L. Burt in 1916. Chapter I is called A New Winnebago. Sahwah the Sunfish sits atop the diving tower. Through Nakwisi's spy-glass she squints at the distant horizon. Migwan calls up from the rocks below: Sister Anne, do you see any one coming?

No sign of the Bluebird yet, Sahwah answers. If Gladys doesn't come soon she shall die of impatience. What will the new girl be like? She is going to be my affinity, Migwan feels it in her bones. Sahwah sighs that nobody in her right mind would choose her for an affinity; she is not interesting enough looking. You see somebody for the first time, know nothing of her, and something tells you the two of you belong together.
the-hawaiian-archipelago:
Isabella L. Bird wrote The Hawaiian Archipelago, letters about six months among the palm groves, coral reefs, and volcanoes of the Sandwich Islands. Bird explains in a preface that she landed while traveling for health, stayed nearly seven months, and rode on horseback across the islands. She climbed high mountains, visited active volcanoes, and lived among the people of the islands.

Bird says friends urged her to publish because older books dealt mainly with customs now gone and with early mission history. Her letters, written to her sister, aim to keep the fresh feel of what she saw. She gives close attention to daily life, travel on rough ground, and the volcano of Mauna Loa, which she saw in good conditions.
the-long-ago:
Jacob William Wright's The Long Ago gathers twelve short pieces with plain titles. They include The Garden, The River, Christmas, Butter, Eggs, Ducks, and Geese. The Sugar Barrels, Jimmy the Lamplighter, Flies, Grandmother, and When Day is Done complete the set. The opening finds the narrator at a private office window in the early evening, gray-templed and pressed by the day's concerns, while trolley-cars and wagons surge below. As he watches, the city slowly changes.

Tall buildings fade into elm trees over a dusty lane, trolley-bells soften into the tinkle of a homeward herd, and he is trudging a country road again beside the reader. Wright writes nostalgic sketches in which adult city life keeps dissolving into boyhood memory, guided by what he calls the Voice of Boyhood.
the-lost-word-a-christmas-legend-of-long:
Henry Van Dyke wrote The Lost Word, a Christmas legend of long ago, published in New York in 1898 and dedicated to his friend Hamilton W. Mabie. Its six parts follow Hermas through poverty, a Christmas loss, riches without rest, and recovered joy. Part one opens in a street of Antioch fifteen hundred years ago, in the dusk of early morning, where young men call up to their fellow student Hermas.

"Come down, Hermas, come down! The night is past. Christ is born to-day." The callers are candidates who have nearly finished two years of training for the Christian church. Their voices ring with glad life and friendly triumph at being awake first. Van Dyke sets a gentle, reflective Christmas tale in the early church, built around a young man's spiritual testing.
the-memoirs-of-victor-hugo: Victor Hugo's Memoirs show only their contents here, so the memoir text itself does not appear. The contents promise eyewitness accounts of the execution of Louis XVI and Napoleon's arrival in Paris in 1815. Sections follow on visions of the real, the theatre, the Academy, and the Tuileries between 1844 and 1848. A long final section covers the Revolution of 1848, from the days of February to Louis Philippe in exile and debates on the days of June.
the-story-of-dago: Annie Fellows Johnston, author of The Little Colonel, wrote this children's story, illustrated by Etheldred B. Barry and published by L. C. Page and Company of Boston in 1900. Only the title pages are present here, with her dedication. She dedicates the book to Gin the Monk. The monkey's pranks lived in the boyhood memories of Dr. Gavin Fulton. The tale of Dago itself does not appear.
the-story-of-little-black-mingo:
A picture story tells of an orphan girl. The author also wrote The Story of Little Black Sambo. No name is printed on the pages present here. The girl lives with an old woman called Black Noggy. Noggy is horrid and cross. Noggy scolds Mingo daily and sometimes beats her with a stick, though she has done nothing naughty.

Mingo goes to the river to fill a water pot. A huge Mugger ambushes her there. The crocodile bursts through the bottom of the pot. It announces that it will eat her up. The broken pot catches round the creature's neck and slows its paws, so she escapes, only for Noggy to accuse her of breaking the pot herself and threaten another beating.
warwick-woodlands-things-as-they-were-th:
Frank Forester wrote The Warwick Woodlands, or Things as They Were Twenty Years Ago, as a sporting tale of old friends met again. On a fine October evening the narrator sits on the back stoop of a cheerful bachelor's house in Mercer Street, New York. His old comrade Henry Archer sits with him. Many frowns and smiles of fortune, he says, the two had weathered together. No stauncher friend, merrier companion, or keener sportsman ever lived, he says, than Harry.

They had parted in St. James's Street almost ten years before. One bound west, and one for the eastern world. Archer went west to clear trees and raise log huts in Canada's backwoods. The narrator went east, to shoot tigers in the Carnatic and drink arrack punch. From that reunion the tale rides out to the Warwick woods.
